title: Agent Coders Clinic
text:
0.1 What is the Agent Coders Clinic?
The Agent Coders Clinic is a hands-on workshop where you’ll learn to use AI coding agents — tools that can read your files, run commands, edit code, and work through multi-step tasks on your behalf. Whether this is your first time using an AI coding tool or you’ve been experimenting on your own, this clinic will give you a practical workflow you can take back to your daily work.

title: Agent Coders Clinic
text:
0.2 What you’ll learn
By the end of this clinic, you will:

Understand what an agentic coding harness is and how it differs from chatbots or autocomplete
Connect to a shared gateway that gives you access to Claude and open-source models — no accounts or subscriptions needed
Practice a clear–handoff–notes workflow that keeps your work organized across sessions
Try a group activity where an agent analyzes a real GitHub repository
Learn how to write SKILLS.md files that teach an agent reusable tasks

title: Agent Coders Clinic
text:
0.3 The environment
Everything runs on a sandboxed JupyterHub. You have a terminal, a file browser, and your choice of coding tool. Nothing connects to private or confidential systems — this is a safe space for learning and experimenting.

title: Agent Coders Clinic
text:
0.4 Agenda







Time
Topic




First half
Setup, intro to agentic coding, core workflow (clear / handoff / notes)


Second half
Group activity (repo reproducibility analysis), SKILLS.md

title: Agent Coders Clinic
text:
0.5 Ready?
Start with Setup & Connection to get your tools connected.

title: 2  Setup & Connection
text:
2.1 What you need
Two things from the organizer:
Your key has its own spending limit and expiry date. Keep it to yourself.

title: 2  Setup & Connection
text:
Gateway URL — the address of the shared gateway
Personal key — starts with sk-, sent to you privately

title: 2  Setup & Connection
text:
2.2 Set your environment variables
In a terminal, run:
export GATEWAY_KEY=sk-your-key-here
export GATEWAY_URL=https://your-gateway-url-here
These last only for this terminal session. If you open a new terminal, run both lines again.

title: 2  Setup & Connection
text:
2.3 Connect your tool
Pick the tool you want to use. You only need one.

2.3.1 Claude Code
Install (if you don’t have it):
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Connect to the gateway:
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=$GATEWAY_URL
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=$GATEWAY_KEY
export ANTHROPIC_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5-20251001
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL=claude-opus-4-6
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL=claude-sonnet-4-6
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5-20251001
If you normally use Claude Code another way (Bedrock, Vertex, or an Anthropic API key), clear those settings so they don’t override the gateway:
unset CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
Start with claude. Type /status to confirm the gateway URL. /model switches models.


2.3.2 OpenCode
Install (if you don’t have it):
npm install -g opencode-ai
Write the config file (this replaces any existing ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json — save a copy first if you have one):
mkdir -p ~/.config/opencode
cat > ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json <<EOF
{
  "\$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "model": "gateway/claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
  "small_model": "gateway/claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
  "provider": {
    "gateway": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "name": "Workshop gateway",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "$GATEWAY_URL/v1",
        "apiKey": "{env:GATEWAY_KEY}"
      },
      "models": {
        "claude-haiku-4-5-20251001": {},
        "claude-sonnet-4-6": {},
        "claude-opus-4-6": {},
        "qwen3-coder-480b": {},
        "qwen3-coder-30b": {},
        "devstral-2": {},
        "kimi-k2.5": {},
        "glm-5": {},
        "minimax-m2.5": {},
        "deepseek-v3.2": {},
        "gpt-oss-120b": {}
      }
    }
  }
}
EOF
Start with opencode. The gateway models are under “Workshop gateway” in /models.


2.3.3 GitHub Copilot CLI
Install (if you don’t have it):
curl -fsSL https://gh.io/copilot-install | bash
Connect to the gateway:
export COPILOT_PROVIDER_TYPE=openai
export COPILOT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL=$GATEWAY_URL/v1
export COPILOT_PROVIDER_API_KEY=$GATEWAY_KEY
export COPILOT_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5-20251001
Start with copilot. To switch models, quit, change COPILOT_MODEL, and restart.

title: 2  Setup & Connection
text:
2.4 Verify it works
Once your tool is running, try a simple prompt:

What directory am I in? List the files here.

If the agent reads your filesystem and responds, you’re connected.

title: 3  Models & Budget
text:
3.2 When to switch models

Haiku — your everyday model. Use it for most tasks.
Sonnet or Opus — reach for these when Haiku struggles: complex reasoning, large refactors, subtle bugs. Switch back when you’re done.
Open models — interesting to try, but they use file-reading and editing tools less reliably than Claude. If one answers without looking at your files, ask it explicitly (e.g., “use the read tool on notes.txt”).

title: 3  Models & Budget
text:
3.3 Switching models

Claude Code: /model claude-sonnet-4-6 (or any model name from the table)
OpenCode: /models, then select from the list
Copilot CLI: quit, change COPILOT_MODEL, restart

title: 3  Models & Budget
text:
3.4 Checking your budget
Run this in a terminal (with GATEWAY_URL and GATEWAY_KEY set):
curl -s $GATEWAY_URL/key/info \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GATEWAY_KEY" |
  python3 -c "
import sys, json
i = json.load(sys.stdin)['info']
print(f\"Spent \${i['spend']:.2f} of \${i['max_budget']:.2f}; expires {i['expires'][:10]}\")
"
Spending shows up about a minute after each request.

title: 3  Models & Budget
text:
3.5 Making your budget last

Stay on Haiku for routine tasks. It’s the best cost-to-capability ratio.
Switch to Sonnet/Opus only when you need to, then switch back.
Use /clear between tasks — this resets the conversation, which means the agent sends less context with each request and each request costs less.
The gateway caches repeated context for Claude models, so later requests in a session cost less than the first one.







Tip



Running /usage in Claude Code shows what the current session has spent.

title: 4  What Is Agentic Coding?
text:
4.1 The idea
You’ve probably used AI chat — you type a question, you get an answer. Maybe you’ve used autocomplete in an editor, where an AI suggests the next few characters as you type.
An agentic coding tool is different. It’s a program — sometimes called an agentic harness — that gives an AI model access to your actual development environment: your files, your terminal, and your git repository. Instead of just answering questions, it can:

title: 4  What Is Agentic Coding?
text:
Read your files to understand your project
Search across your codebase for patterns or definitions
Edit files directly
Run commands in your terminal (with your permission)
Iterate — check its own work, fix mistakes, and keep going

title: 4  What Is Agentic Coding?
text:
4.2 The agent loop
When you give an agentic tool a task, it doesn’t just generate text. It runs a loop:

Think about what to do next
Act — read a file, run a command, make an edit
Observe the result
Repeat until the task is done (or it gets stuck and asks you)

This is why they’re called “agentic” — the model is acting on your behalf, making decisions about what tools to use and in what order.

title: 4  What Is Agentic Coding?
text:
4.3 Examples of agentic harnesses
There are several tools that work this way. In this clinic you can use any of them through the shared gateway:

Claude Code — Anthropic’s CLI tool, built for Claude
OpenCode — open-source, works with Claude and open models
GitHub Copilot CLI — GitHub’s coding tool
Gemini CLI — Google’s coding tool

They all follow the same basic pattern: you give a prompt, the agent works through it using tools, and you review the result. The commands and interface differ, but the concept is the same.

title: 4  What Is Agentic Coding?
text:
4.4 What an agent is not

It’s not magic — agents make mistakes, especially on complex or ambiguous tasks.
It’s not a chatbot — keep interactions focused on tasks, not open-ended conversation.
It doesn’t remember between sessions — that’s why you use handoff notes.
It needs verification — see Checking the Agent’s Work.

title: 5  How to Work with an Agent
text:
5.1 The workflow
An agentic tool is not a chatbot. The biggest mistake people make is treating it like one — free-form messages, tangents, and endless conversations that confuse both you and the agent.
The discipline is simple: one task, one session, one handoff.
flowchart TD
    A["🎯 Pick a task"] --> B["🔍 Plan first"]
    B --> C["🔨 Build small"]
    C --> D{"Done or\nswitching?"}
    D -- Yes --> E["📝 Handoff note\nto notes/"]
    E --> F["/clear"]
    F --> A
    D -- "No, keep going" --> C
That’s the whole thing. Let’s walk through each step.
crumbs: 5  How to Work with an Agent

title: 5  How to Work with an Agent
text:
5.2 Pick a task
Every session starts with a task — something with a clear scope.







Good tasks
Not tasks




“Draft the introduction chapter”
“Help me with my project”


“Figure out why the PDF won’t render”
“Let’s work on stuff”


“Brainstorm what sections this book needs”
“Tell me about Quarto”


“Write tests for the data-loading function”
“Make everything better”



A task can be planning, research, brainstorming, or building. The point is that it has a boundary.
crumbs: 5  How to Work with an Agent

title: 5  How to Work with an Agent
text:
5.3 Plan first, build small
Two rules that save time and money:
Plan before you build. Start by asking the agent to explore and make a plan. Save the plan to notes/. Then clear and start a fresh session to execute. Exploration context clutters implementation.
Build small before building big. One chapter, one function, one section at a time. Review it, then continue. Small pieces are easier to check and cheaper to redo.
crumbs: 5  How to Work with an Agent

title: 5  How to Work with an Agent
text:
5.4 Close the loop
When you’re done with a task — or switching to a different one — or the conversation is just getting long — close it:

Tell the agent: “I’m about to clear. Write a handoff note to notes/ with what we did and what’s next.”
Run /clear
Start the next task fresh

The handoff note is a short file — what was done, what’s next, any decisions made. Not a transcript, not a code dump. A sticky note for the next session.
You don’t have to finish to close. “Got halfway through X, next step is Y” is a perfectly good handoff. The next session picks it up.
crumbs: 5  How to Work with an Agent

title: 5  How to Work with an Agent
text:
5.5 Why this matters






WarningLong conversations cost you three ways




Money — every message resends the entire conversation history
Quality — the agent drifts and loses focus as context piles up
Risk — if the session dies, you lose everything since the last handoff

Short, focused tasks with handoff notes between them are cheaper, more reliable, and easier to pick up later — by you or by someone else on your team.
crumbs: 5  How to Work with an Agent

title: 5  How to Work with an Agent
text:
5.6 What about /resume?
Most tools can resume the previous session. This works for short interruptions — you stepped away for coffee and want to continue the same task.
But for picking up work after a longer gap, or when someone else is taking over, start fresh:

Read the notes in notes/ and continue where we left off.

This gives the agent exactly the context it needs and nothing it doesn’t. And anyone on the team can pick it up — not just the person who started it.
crumbs: 5  How to Work with an Agent

title: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent
text:
6.1 Before you start
In this activity you’ll practice the full clear–handoff–notes workflow from Skills 101. You’ll use an AI coding agent to plan and execute edits to a real Quarto book — the same template this documentation is built on.
crumbs: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent

title: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent
text:
6.1.1 1. Create your own copy of the template
Go to https://github.com/nmfs-opensci/NOAA-quarto-book and click the green “Use this template” button to create a copy in your own GitHub account. Make the repo public and check the box to include all branches (so you get the gh-pages branch).


6.1.2 2. Clone it into JupyterHub
In a terminal:
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/NOAA-quarto-book.git
cd NOAA-quarto-book


6.1.3 3. Start your agent
Launch your coding tool inside the cloned repo:
claude
(Or opencode, copilot, etc. — whichever you set up.)
crumbs: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent

title: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent
text:
6.2 Phase 1: Plan the edits
Goal: Have the agent explore the book and help you plan what to change. Save the plan to notes/. Then clear.

6.2.1 What to do
Ask the agent to look at the book and help you come up with a plan for turning it into something of your own — a project page, a lab notebook, workshop notes, whatever you like. For example:

Read the files in this Quarto book and help me plan how to turn it into [a guide for my lab / notes for my project / a workshop site]. What chapters should I add, remove, or rename? What needs to change in _quarto.yml?

Work with the agent to refine the plan. Go back and forth until you’re happy with it.


6.2.2 Save the plan
When the plan feels ready:

Create a notes/ directory and save our plan to notes/plan.md.



6.2.3 Clear
You’ve finished phase 1. The plan is on disk. Tell the agent you’re about to clear:

I’m about to clear this session. Is there anything else we should save to notes/ before I do?

Then clear:
/clear






Tip



Why clear now? The conversation has gotten long — you’ve been exploring files and discussing options. Clearing resets the context so your next requests are cheaper and more focused. The plan in notes/ has everything the agent needs to continue.
crumbs: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent

title: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent
text:
6.3 Phase 2: Execute the plan (Draft 1)
Goal: Have the agent read the plan and execute it. Think about how to approach the work. Clear when done, with a handoff note.

6.3.1 Pick up the plan
Start a fresh prompt:

Read notes/plan.md and the current book structure. We’re going to execute this plan to create a first draft.



6.3.2 Think about how to execute
Before diving in, consider: should you ask the agent to do everything at once, or go step by step?
All at once works when:

The plan is clear and specific
Changes are independent (renaming chapters doesn’t depend on writing content)
You trust the agent to make reasonable choices

Step by step works better when:

You want to review as you go
Steps depend on each other (write chapter 1 before chapter 2 references it)
You’re not sure how the agent will interpret something

A reasonable middle ground: ask the agent to do a logical group of changes, review, then continue. For example:

Start by updating _quarto.yml with the new chapter structure from the plan. Don’t write the chapter content yet — just set up the structure.

Then after reviewing:

Now write first drafts of the new chapters.



6.3.3 Do the work
Execute the plan however you chose. Review what the agent produces. Ask it to fix anything that’s off.


6.3.4 Render and check
When the draft is done:

Render the book with quarto render and check for errors. Fix any problems.



6.3.5 Clear with a handoff note
You’ve finished draft 1. Before clearing, have the agent write a handoff:

Write a handoff note to notes/handoff.md. Summarize what we did, what the book looks like now, and what still needs work.

Review the handoff note — does it capture everything the next session would need? Then clear:
/clear
crumbs: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent

title: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent
text:
6.4 Phase 3: Wrap up
Goal: Practice picking up from a handoff note, then leave a final handoff for what’s next.

6.4.1 Resume from the handoff
Start a fresh prompt:

Read the notes in notes/ and tell me where we are with this book.

The agent should be able to orient itself from the handoff note and tell you the current state without you having to re-explain anything.


6.4.2 Leave a final handoff

Update the handoff note in notes/ with what’s left to do and where to find the information needed to finish. This is the end of the clinic session.
crumbs: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent

title: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent
text:
6.5 Discussion
After the activity, think about:

Did clearing and resuming work? Could the agent pick up from the handoff note without losing important context?
How did you break up the work? All at once vs. step by step — what worked better?
What made a good handoff note? What was missing? What was unnecessary?
How would this workflow help in your real work? Think about projects that span multiple days or involve handoffs between people.







Note



The point of this activity isn’t to produce a perfect book — it’s to practice the workflow. A messy first draft with clean handoff notes is a better outcome than a polished book with no notes.
crumbs: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent

title: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
7.1 The problem
AI coding agents don’t remember anything between sessions. When you start a new session — or run /clear — the agent has no idea what you were doing five minutes ago. It starts fresh every time.
You might think the solution is to build up a huge memory file that the agent loads at the start of every session. But that creates its own problems: the file gets long, stale, and full of context the agent doesn’t need for the current task. It wastes budget re-reading old information.
There’s a simpler approach.
crumbs: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
7.2 The workflow: clear, handoff, notes
The core habit is three steps:

7.2.1 1. Work on a task
Start your agent and give it something to do. As it works, it builds up conversation context — the files it has read, the decisions it has made, the changes it has written.


7.2.2 2. Before you stop: handoff
When you’re done with a task (or switching to something else), tell the agent:

Write a handoff note to notes/ summarizing what you did, what’s left, and any decisions you made.

The agent creates a short file — like notes/handoff-2026-09-29.md — capturing exactly what the next session needs to know.


7.2.3 3. Clear and continue
Run /clear (or close the session). The conversation context is gone, but the handoff note is on disk.
Next time, start the agent and say:

Read the notes in notes/ and pick up where we left off.

The agent reads the handoff, gets oriented, and continues the work.
crumbs: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
section: 7.3 What goes in a handoff note
text:
7.3 What goes in a handoff note
Good handoff notes are short and specific:

What was done (in a sentence or two)
What’s next (the immediate next step)
Any decisions made that aren’t obvious from the code
Blockers or open questions
crumbs: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
section: 7.4 What does NOT go in a handoff note
text:
7.4 What does NOT go in a handoff note

Entire file contents — the agent can read files itself
Code dumps — the code is in the repo
Full project history — keep it to what’s relevant right now
Anything the agent can figure out by looking at the repo







Tip



Think of a handoff note like a sticky note for a colleague: “I finished X, next step is Y, watch out for Z.”
crumbs: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
7.5 Example
Here’s what a handoff note might look like:
# Handoff — 2026-09-29

## Done
- Set up Quarto book structure for clinic docs
- Wrote first drafts of setup and models chapters

## Next
- Write the "What Is Agentic Coding?" chapter
- Review setup chapter against latest participant-quickstart.md

## Decisions
- Dropped PDF/docx output for now — HTML only until content stabilizes
- Using parts in _quarto.yml to group chapters into sections
crumbs: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
7.6 Why /clear matters
Every message you send includes the entire conversation so far. As the conversation grows, each request sends more tokens and costs more. Running /clear resets this — your next request is cheap again.
The handoff note means you don’t lose anything important. You trade a long, expensive conversation for a short, focused one with a lightweight file to get the agent back up to speed.
crumbs: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
7.7 The notes/ directory
Keep handoff notes and working notes in a notes/ directory in your project. This keeps them separate from your actual project files and easy to find.
Some things that work well in notes/:

Handoff notes (handoff-YYYY-MM-DD.md)
Plans and task lists for ongoing work
Analysis summaries from agent tasks (like the reproducibility analysis)
crumbs: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
7.8 Branches and PRs
Once you’re comfortable with clear/handoff/notes, you can add git branches and pull requests to the workflow:

Create a branch for a task
Do the work (with clear/handoff as needed)
Open a PR when it’s ready
Merge and move on

This is a natural complement — the branch keeps your changes isolated and reviewable, and the handoff notes help you (or someone else) pick up the work if it spans multiple sessions. But the clear/handoff/notes habit is the foundation. Get that down first.
crumbs: 7  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 8  Agent Skills 102: SKILLS.md
text:
8.1 What is SKILLS.md?
A SKILLS.md file lives in your project and teaches the agent reusable tasks — things you do repeatedly that you want done the same way every time. Instead of re-explaining a process in every session, you write it once in SKILLS.md and the agent follows it.
Think of it as a recipe book for your agent.

title: 8  Agent Skills 102: SKILLS.md
text:
8.2 How it works
When you tell an agent to use a skill, it reads SKILLS.md, finds the matching section, and follows those instructions. For example:

Use the “render-check” skill to build and verify the book.

The agent looks up “render-check” in SKILLS.md and executes the steps.

title: 8  Agent Skills 102: SKILLS.md
text:
8.3 Writing a skill
A skill is a section in SKILLS.md with a clear name and step-by-step instructions. Keep them concrete and specific.

8.3.1 Example: render-check
## render-check

Render the Quarto book and check for problems.

1. Run `quarto render` in the project root
2. Check the output for errors or warnings
3. If there are errors, read the error message and fix the issue
4. Re-render until it builds cleanly
5. Report what you fixed (if anything)


8.3.2 Example: format-bib
## format-bib

Clean up the bibliography file.

1. Read `content/references.bib`
2. Check each entry for:
   - Missing fields (author, title, year, journal/publisher)
   - Inconsistent formatting (e.g., mixed use of curly braces)
   - Duplicate entries (same DOI or matching author+title+year)
3. Fix any issues found
4. Sort entries alphabetically by citation key


8.3.3 Example: daily-handoff
## daily-handoff

Write an end-of-session handoff note.

1. Summarize what was done in this session
2. List what should happen next
3. Note any decisions or blockers
4. Save to `notes/handoff-YYYY-MM-DD.md` using today's date

title: 8  Agent Skills 102: SKILLS.md
text:
8.4 Tips for writing skills

Be specific. “Check for problems” is vague. “Run quarto render and check for errors” is actionable.
Use numbered steps. The agent follows them in order.
Include the actual commands. Don’t make the agent guess what to run.
Keep them short. A skill that’s a full page long is probably two skills.
Name them clearly. You’ll invoke them by name.

title: 8  Agent Skills 102: SKILLS.md
text:
8.5 Where to put SKILLS.md
Put it in the root of your project, next to CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. The agent will find it when it reads your project files.

title: 8  Agent Skills 102: SKILLS.md
text:
8.6 SKILLS.md vs. CLAUDE.md









CLAUDE.md
SKILLS.md




Purpose
Project context and conventions
Reusable task recipes


When it’s read
Automatically at session start
When you invoke a skill


Contents
Build commands, architecture, coding style
Step-by-step procedures



Both are useful. CLAUDE.md gives the agent background knowledge. SKILLS.md gives it specific procedures to follow on demand.

title: 9  Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent’s Work
text:
9.1 The problem with “just review it”
Every guide to AI coding tools says “always review what the agent produces.” That’s true, but it’s not very helpful advice — especially when the agent is writing code you couldn’t have written yourself, or making changes across many files at once.
If you’re a scientist learning to code with an agent, the agent may genuinely be a better coder than you are. So how do you verify work you don’t fully understand?
crumbs: 9  Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent's Work

title: 9  Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent’s Work
section: 9.2 You don’t have to understand every line
text:
9.2 You don’t have to understand every line
Verification isn’t about reading every line of code and confirming it’s correct. It’s about checking that the thing works the way you expect it to. You’re the domain expert — you know what the output should look like, what the data means, and what would be wrong.
Good verification questions:

Does it run without errors?
Does the output look right to me — someone who knows this data / this domain?
Did it change anything I didn’t ask it to change?
Can I explain what this does (even if I couldn’t have written it)?
crumbs: 9  Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent's Work

title: 9  Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent’s Work
section: 9.3 Let the agent break things for you
text:
9.3 Let the agent break things for you
Here’s the key insight: you don’t have to be the one who finds the bugs. You can get the agent to stress-test its own work — if you give it the right information.

9.3.1 Give it real data
The agent probably wrote the code using example data or assumptions about your data. Give it the real thing:

Here’s our actual dataset: data/survey-2024.csv. Run the analysis on this and show me the output. Does anything look wrong?

Real data has edge cases — missing values, unexpected formats, outliers — that break fragile code.


9.3.2 Tell it what you know
You’re the domain expert. You know things the agent doesn’t — what reasonable values look like, what relationships should exist in the data, what the previous version produced. Feed that knowledge in:

The count column should never be negative. Are there any negative values in the output?


Last year’s report had 342 sites. If we’re getting a very different number, something is probably wrong.


This function is supposed to handle both CSV and Excel files. Try it with data/samples.xlsx — does it work?



9.3.3 Ask it to write tests
You don’t have to write the tests yourself. But you can tell the agent what to test for:

Write tests that check:

The function handles empty input without crashing
Missing values in the date column don’t cause errors
The output has the same number of rows as the input
Column names match what downstream code expects


You’re providing the domain knowledge about what should be true. The agent provides the testing mechanics.


9.3.4 Ask it to try to break it
This is one of the most useful things you can do:

Try to break this. What inputs would cause it to fail? What assumptions is it making that might not hold?

Agents are good at this — they can reason about edge cases and generate adversarial inputs. Breaking things is good. Every failure reveals something that needs to be more robust.
crumbs: 9  Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent's Work

title: 9  Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent’s Work
text:
9.4 A verification workflow
A practical approach:

Does it run? Ask the agent to execute it. Fix any errors.
Does it look right? Review the output with your domain knowledge. Flag anything suspicious.
Feed it real data. Swap in your actual files and see what happens.
Ask it to break it. Have the agent find its own bugs.
Check the diff. Before committing, look at what files changed. Anything unexpected?







Tip



Verification works best as a separate task. After the agent builds something, clear the session, then start a new session focused entirely on testing and breaking what was built. A fresh session means the agent isn’t biased by the decisions it made during implementation.
crumbs: 9  Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent's Work

title: 9  Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent’s Work
section: 9.5 This is a skill you build over time
text:
9.5 This is a skill you build over time
Nobody gets this right immediately. The more you work with agents, the better you get at:

Knowing what questions to ask
Spotting when output “looks off”
Giving the agent the right information to test against

For now, the most important habit is: don’t just accept what the agent produces. Run it, look at it, and throw some real data at it before you call it done.

title: 10  Tool Comparison
text:
10.2 Key differences
Claude Code is the most full-featured for this clinic. It has built-in commands for managing context (/clear), checking status (/status, /usage), and switching models (/model). It’s designed around Claude and works well with CLAUDE.md project files.
OpenCode is open-source and has the most flexible model configuration. It works well with both Claude and open models through the gateway. Good if you want to compare models side by side.
GitHub Copilot CLI is straightforward to set up. To switch models you need to quit and restart with a different COPILOT_MODEL environment variable. No GitHub account needed when using the gateway.
Gemini CLI is Google’s tool. It follows the same agentic pattern. Configuration is via environment variables.

title: 10  Tool Comparison
text:
10.3 Common commands across tools
Regardless of which tool you use, you’ll do the same basic things:

Give a prompt — type what you want the agent to do
Approve tool use — most tools ask permission before editing files or running commands
Review output — always check what the agent did before moving on
End the session — close the tool or clear context when switching tasks

title: 11  Troubleshooting
text: 11.1 Connection problems

title: 11  Troubleshooting
text:
11.1.1 “Authentication error” or “Invalid API key”
Your GATEWAY_KEY is wrong or not set in this terminal.
echo $GATEWAY_KEY
If it’s empty, set it again:
export GATEWAY_KEY=sk-your-key-here


11.1.2 “Connection refused” or timeout
The gateway server may be stopped. Check with the organizer.
Also verify your GATEWAY_URL is set:
echo $GATEWAY_URL


11.1.3 Claude Code ignores the gateway
If you have other Claude Code settings (Bedrock, Vertex, or an Anthropic API key), they can override the gateway. Clear them:
unset CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
Then set the gateway variables again and restart claude.

title: 11  Troubleshooting
text:
11.2 Budget problems

11.2.1 “Budget exceeded”
Your key has hit its spending limit. Ask the organizer — they can increase it or issue a new key.


11.2.2 “Key expired” or “Key blocked”
The key’s time limit is up, or it was switched off. Ask the organizer for a new one.


11.2.3 How to check your remaining budget
curl -s $GATEWAY_URL/key/info \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GATEWAY_KEY" |
  python3 -c "
import sys, json
i = json.load(sys.stdin)['info']
print(f\"Spent \${i['spend']:.2f} of \${i['max_budget']:.2f}; expires {i['expires'][:10]}\")
"

title: 11  Troubleshooting
text:
11.3 Agent behavior problems

11.3.1 Agent gives generic answers without reading files
Some models (especially open models) don’t use file-reading tools reliably. Try:

Being explicit: “Use the read tool to look at README.md, then answer.”
Switching to a Claude model, which handles tool use more reliably.



11.3.2 Agent seems confused or stuck
The conversation may have gotten too long. Run /clear and start fresh. If you have handoff notes in notes/, tell the agent to read those for context.


11.3.3 Agent makes changes you didn’t ask for
Review what the agent is doing before approving. Most tools ask permission before writing files. If it’s going off track, interrupt it and clarify what you actually want.

title: 11  Troubleshooting
text:
11.4 Environment variables cheat sheet
If things aren’t working, check that all the right variables are set:
echo "GATEWAY_URL: $GATEWAY_URL"
echo "GATEWAY_KEY: $GATEWAY_KEY"
echo "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL: $ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL"
echo "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN: $ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN"
echo "ANTHROPIC_MODEL: $ANTHROPIC_MODEL"
For Claude Code, ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL should match GATEWAY_URL and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN should match GATEWAY_KEY.
